newsitem.title: KAZAKHSTAN: FOCUS-Kazakh govt to extend domestic debt maturity. [CORRECTED 09:50 GMT]
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Kazakh govt to extend domestic debt maturity. [CORRECTED 09:50 GMT]

text.p: Kazakhstan said on Thursday it would extend the maturity of its domestic debt in a bid to bring back foreign investors and local banks put off by a steep fall in yields on existing papers.

"Now we are turning to longer debt issues -- two- and three-year securities. These will be discount papers like current Treasury bills, and will also be sold at auctions," Finance Minister Alexander Pavlov told Reuters.
"The first auction will be held this month," he said.

Central bank chairman Uraz Dzhandosov said he did not expect any restrictions on foreign investment in the new bills. Foreigners are entitled to buy up to 30 percent of Kazakhstan's existing three-, six- and 12-month T-bills.

Yields these bills have fallen sharply over the last few months, and many local banks and foreign investors -- once keen buyers of Kazakh government securities -- are eyeing T-bill markets in other countries.

"Foreign investors are now much less interested in buying Kazakh T-bills. They are turning to Russian and Ukrainian papers which pay much higher yields," Oleg Tsurkan, head treasurer at ABN AMRO Bank Kazakhstan, told Reuters on Wednesday.
"Foreigners' participation in the last two T-bill auctions was small," Dzhandosov told Reuters. "I believe we will not impose any limits (for foreign investment) on two- and three-year securities."

The yield on Kazakh 12-month MKM discount T-bills fell to 15.74 percent annual on Monday, from 22.59 percent annual at the last auction on May 6. Three-month paper fell on Tuesday to 10.30 percent from 12.29 percent on May 27.

While yields on Russian and Ukrainian T-bills average over 20 percent annual, Kazakh banks complain that annualised yields on Kazakh papers are lower than inflation, which the central bank targets at 17 percent this year.
Dealers say yields plunge on high demand because there are no alternatives to the existing T-bills (corrects to insert dropped word "no").
Banks also prefer low T-bill yields to risky loans to the shaky economy.
"I agree that this is abnormal when T-bill yields are lower than inflation," Pavlov said. "This is why we are going to issue these two- and three-year papers."

Dzhandosov said the volume of each issue of the new T-bills would total between 500 million and one billion tenge. He said auctions would be regular but declined to name the date of the first one or to say how often the new securities would be sold.
